1. The conservation law f⁴ + g⁴ = 1 holds
2. The shifted functions (f(x+L), g(x+L)) also satisfy the ODE if f(L)=1, g(L)=0
3. By uniqueness, f(x+L) = f(x) and g(x+L) = g(x)
4. We need to show f returns to (1,0) at some positive L

Looking at this problem, I need to prove that for any set of n real numbers, there exists a non-empty subset S and integer m such that |m + sum(S)| ≤ 1/(n+1).

The key idea is the pigeonhole principle on partial sums: consider n+1 partial sums p(0)=0, p(1)=x_1, ..., p(n)=x_1+...+x_n. Look at their fractional parts modulo 1/(n+1). By pigeonhole, two of them fall in the same interval [k/(n+1), (k+1)/(n+1)), so their difference (which is a partial sum of consecutive elements) is within 1/(n+1) of an integer.
